claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering temperatures above 2300 °C.
The starting ZrB2 powder has inherent surface oxides.
Conventionally processed ZrB2 has limitations in densification.
A silicate-precursor coating on ZrB2 particles converts into a sub-micron borosilicate glass phase during sintering.
The coated ZrB2 can be sintered under vacuum at about 2200 °C and approximately 40 MPa.
An appropriate dwell time permits precursor-to-glass conversion without excessive grain growth.
The intervention forms an in situ borosilicate glass phase at ZrB2 particle interfaces.
The interfacial glass provides a transient liquid-like medium that enhances diffusion and densification.
The interfacial glass acts as a continuous barrier to liquid-metal infiltration during service.
The borosilicate glass facilitates particle rearrangement and mass transport at lower sintering temperatures.
The glass phase fills microscopic voids and covers potential defect sites.
Filling voids and covering defect sites reduces pore nucleation.
The glass phase inhibits corrosion-induced damage during exposure to liquid plating baths.
The modified ZrB2 is expected to achieve full densification at about 2200 °C.
The modified ZrB2 is expected to have a nearly pore-free, high-density microstructure.
The modified ZrB2 is expected to resist corrosion and hole formation better than conventionally prepared ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C usually has higher porosity and more microstructural defects.
Porosity and microstructural defects in conventionally processed ZrB2 are prone to prolonged liquid-metal attack.
